### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary When any GPU kernel on the main stream never terminates, the EngineCore parks forever in `AsyncModelRunnerOutput.get_output()` → `copy_event.synchronize()` — **there is no timeout, no diagnostic, and no recovery**. The engine process stays alive, `/health` keeps returning 200, engine logs go silent, and SIGTERM is ignored (SIGKILL required). In our production fleet this presented as inference instances serving nothing for **14 hours undetected**. The concrete kernel that triggered this for us was flashinfer 0.6.13's `RadixTopKMaskLogitsKernel_MultiCTA` deadlocking on its inter-CTA barrier on SM120 under multi-process GPU contention (details below). That kernel bug is **already fixed** in flashinfer 0.6.16.post3 (bundled from v0.27.0) — we verified our reproducer no longer fires there. **This issue is about vLLM's behavior while the kernel was stuck**, which is unchanged through v0.27.1 and will recur identically with the next never-terminating kernel from any library: ``` # both runners park the same way (captured with py-spy on wedged engines): Thread (idle): "MainThread" synchronize torch/cuda/streams.py:254 ← blocks forever, no timeout get_output vllm/v1/worker/gpu/async_utils.py:50 (V2 runner) — or — vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:301 (V1 runner) result vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:38 step_with_batch_queue vllm/v1/engine/core.py:595 ``` Aggravating detail: `_process_aborts_queue()` is the statement immediately after the blocking `result()` in `step_with_batch_queue`, so queued request aborts are never drained once the engine parks — cancellations pile up invisibly. ## How we hit it (production + controlled reproduction) - Production: upgrading 0.22.1 → 0.25.1 flipped our dense Gemma-3/Gemma-4-class models to configurations whose per-step top-k/top-p sampling runs flashinfer's multi-CTA radix kernel. On GPUs shared by several busy instances (time-sliced, no MPS/MIG), three instances wedged the same evening. GPU signature during the wedge: **100% SM utilization at ~100 W with ~0% memory throughput** — a spinning kernel, confirmed with cuda-gdb attached to three independent wedged engines (twice V2 runner, once V1): ``` 0x... in void flashinfer::sampling::RadixTopKMaskLogitsKernel_MultiCTA<1024u, 4u, false, float, int>(...)<<<(88,1,1),(1024,1,1)>>> () Kernel Dev Grid Status GridDim BlockDim Invocation * 0 0 313947 Active ... (88,1,1) (1024,1,1) RadixTopKMaskLogitsKernel_MultiCTA... # SASS at PC: LDG → CCTL.IVALL → YIELD → ISETP.GE → @!P4 BRA (spin re-reading a # RadixRowState arrival counter that never reaches its target) ``` - Controlled reproduction (fires in 1–6 rounds): two `vllm serve` instances of a dense model on ONE SM120 GPU, requests carrying top_k=64/top_p=0.95; per round, against both simultaneously: 250 streaming requests (deep queue via --max-num-seqs 8) → RST-abort all connections at once → repeat → 8 fresh streaming requests. Results across configurations: | configuration (identical dual-instance load) | result | |---|---| | v0.25.1, V2 runner (default) | both engines wedged, round 1 | | v0.25.1, V1 runner (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`) | both wedged, rounds 4 and 6 | | v0.25.1, `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0` | 15/15 + 15/15 clean | | v0.27.1 (flashinfer 0.6.16.post3), sampler ON, V2 | 15/15 + 15/15 clean | Single-instance soak (60 rounds across three engine configurations) never reproduced — the trigger needs multi-process contention, which is also why CI would not see it. ## What I expected A GPU operation that never completes should surface as a loud engine failure within some bounded time — not an engine that accepts connections, reports healthy, ignores SIGTERM, and generates nothing forever. ## Asks 1. **A bounded wait + diagnostic around `AsyncModelRunnerOutput.get_output()`** (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/async_utils.py` and the V1 twin in `gpu_model_runner.py`). Even a generous multi-minute timeout that logs the stall and aborts the engine would turn a silent multi-hour outage into a fast-failing restart that orchestration can see. The sampler deadlock is fixed, but this failure mode is generic: any future stuck kernel (from any library) reproduces it. 2. For released 0.25.x / 0.26.x on SM120 (bundled flashinfer ≤0.6.15): consider a release-note warning recommending `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0` under multi-process GPU sharing, and/or merging #44405 for those class of GPUs. ## Related — this failure genus keeps recurring with different kernels Searching for prior reports turned up at least four open issues with the same signature (GPU kernel never terminates → engine wedges silently → health endpoints keep lying), each with a different trigger: - #43885 — GB10, v0.21.0: engine stuck in `get_output()` on a stuck CUDA stream, GPU 96% util at abnormally low power; reporter built the same external watchdog-restart mitigation we did - #40350 — B200/B300 NVFP4 MoE: silently stops generating under concurrency, `/metrics` 200, hangs until externally killed - #49203 — GB10 hybrid model: intermittent livelock, 96% util, 0 tok/s, no crash, no Xid - #50880 — B300, v0.25.1: 100% SM, 0 tok/s, `/health` 200 (different thread state from ours) - #48720 (RFC) — proposes a step-consensus deadlock guard for TP; adjacent in spirit to ask 1 below None of them identifies its kernel; ours does (cuda-gdb capture + SASS), which is why we can show the engine-side behavior is independent of which kernel gets stuck. A bounded wait at the one choke point every one of these reports flows through (`AsyncModelRunnerOutput.get_output()` and its V1 twin) would convert this whole class from silent multi-hour outages into visible fast failures. Kernel-specific references for OUR trigger: - #42987 / #43013 — same flashinfer kernel hanging on SM120 (RTX 5090) at startup (`_dummy_sampler_run`); ours is the runtime variant under multi-process contention - #44405 (open) — default-disable FlashInfer sampler on SM120/SM121 - flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4131 / flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3625 (open) — remaining multi-CTA barrier fixes - Full artifacts available: py-spy dumps, cuda-gdb kernel focus + SASS disassembly of the spin loop, per-process SM utilization, and the load generator (stdlib-only Python). Happy to attach or test candidate patches — we have the affected hardware and a reproducer that fires within minutes on 0.25.1.

signals.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4 encoder emits an empty `<think></think>` block for assistant turns without reasoning
signals.text: ### Your current environment Affects the `deepseek_v4` tokenizer mode on current `main`. Reproduces with the encoder alone — no GPU or model weights needed. ### 🐛 Describe the bug `vllm/tokenizers/deepseek_v4_encoding.py` renders an assistant turn that carries no `reasoning` as a literal empty thinking block, `<｜Assistant｜><think></think>`. This happens whenever tools are declared. `encode_messages` force-disables `drop_thinking` in that case: ```python if any(m.get("tools") for m in full_messages): effective_drop_thinking = False ``` so every prior assistant turn keeps its thinking block — but if the client did not send `reasoning` back for a turn, there is nothing to put in it. **Reproducer** (encoder only): ```python from vllm.tokenizers.deepseek_v4_encoding import encode_messages tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}}}] msgs = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant.", "tools": tools}, {"role": "user", "content": "Weather?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "On it."}, # no `reasoning` field {"role": "user", "content": "And tomorrow?"}, ] print(encode_messages(msgs, thinking_mode="thinking", reasoning_effort="high")) ``` Actual: ``` ...<｜User｜>Weather?<｜Assistant｜><think></think>On it.<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>... ``` Expected: ``` ...<｜User｜>Weather?<｜Assistant｜></think>On it.<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>... ``` ### Why the chat-style form is the right one `<think></think>` appears in **none** of the four expected outputs shipped with the checkpoint, while the chat-style close is attested in them — including in a `thinking_mode="thinking"` case that is hard-asserted: - [`encoding/tests/test_output_2.txt`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/blob/main/encoding/tests/test_output_2.txt) begins `<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜>You are a helpful assistant.<｜User｜>Hello<｜Assistant｜></think>Hi there! ...` and [`test_encoding_dsv4.py`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/blob/main/encoding/test_encoding_dsv4.py) asserts `encode_messages(messages, thinking_mode="thinking") == gold` for it. - The reference encoder's own `drop_thinking` path produces the same form: for a turn before the last user message it emits `<｜Assistant｜></think>{content}`. - [`encoding/README.md`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/blob/main/encoding/README.md) documents `</think>` placed directly after `<｜Assistant｜>` to close the block immediately. So the reference encoding has two spellings for one and the same situation — "thinking mode, assistant turn whose reasoning is not rendered". The `drop_thinking` spelling is attested and tested; the tools spelling is neither. None of the four fixtures exercises `tools present + reasoning absent`: the two cases that declare tools have reasoning on every assistant turn, and the case with absent reasoning is `thinking_mode="chat"`. ### Observed impact In a long tool-calling conversation where a client does not echo `reasoning` back, these blocks accumulate. In one ~336k-token conversation with 104 of them (the last 17 assistant turns consecutive), the model emitted `</think>` as its very first generated token and produced no reasoning at all, on every sample. Re-encoding only those turns chat-style — with nothing else changed — restored reasoning (0 → several hundred chars). Output quality past that point degraded too, though that had additional contributing factors and is not the claim here. The narrow, verifiable claim: the encoder emits a token sequence that is absent from the reference's expected outputs, in a case those outputs never cover. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] I have searched existing issues and read the docs.

signals.title: [Feature]: Restore length-based speculation skip (speculative max_model_len) or per-request speculative decoding control in V1
signals.text: ## 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch In V0, `--speculative-max-model-len` allowed sequences longer than a threshold to automatically skip speculation (documented in v0.6.x spec_decode docs). In V1, the config plumbing survives — `SpeculativeConfig.max_model_len` is still accepted and `_maybe_override_draft_max_model_len()` still overrides `draft_model_config.max_model_len` (its docstring even says "mainly used for testing that sequences can skip speculation") — but we could not find any runtime consumer under `vllm/v1/`, and empirically the field is a no-op. **Repro (vLLM 0.26.0, DGX Spark GB10, Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4 target + DFlash drafter):** ``` --speculative-config '{"method": "dflash", "model": "z-lab/Qwen3.6-27B-DFlash", "num_speculative_tokens": 10, "max_model_len": 12288}' ``` - Config validation accepts the field, engine boots normally. - A 19,853-token prompt still drafts normally (spec_decode_num_drafts_total +149 for a 150-token completion) — no skip. ## Use case Mixed workloads on a single engine: interactive short prompts get a real speculation win (we measure 1.6–1.8× decode with EAGLE-3/DFlash), but long-document summarization (20K–73K Chinese meeting transcripts) collapses to 5–8% acceptance, making speculation net-negative (decode drops below the no-spec baseline). With no per-request toggle in V1 and the dynamic schedule (`num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size`) keyed on batch size only, there is currently no way to keep speculation for short requests while disabling it for long ones on one engine — and unified-memory hardware (GB10 128GB) cannot co-load a second engine as a workaround. ## Ask Either: 1. Re-implement the V0 behavior: proposers skip drafting when the sequence exceeds the draft model's effective `max_model_len`, or 2. Expose a per-request control (e.g. a SamplingParams / request-level field to disable speculation), or 3. A length-keyed variant of the dynamic speculative schedule. Related: RFC #36657 (Dynamic Speculation Length / confidence-based early exit) addresses the per-step dimension but not the per-request/length dimension. ## Alternatives - Dual serve profiles routed by input length — not viable on unified-memory single-GPU hosts (cannot co-load two large models). - Batch-size-keyed dynamic schedule — wrong dimension for bs=1 long jobs. - Patching the sealed vendor image — not sustainable.

signals.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4 NIXL failure returns corrupted reasoning with empty content
signals.text: ### Your current environment Both roles used the same base image and source overlay. The role-specific model runner and speculative settings were: ```text Base image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.0-cu129-ubuntu2404 Runtime vLLM: 0.26.1rc1.dev657+g793ca6998 Source commit: 793ca6998adfa5a3ab22d6012dee78044b8ba901 Model: DeepSeek-V4 Topology: disaggregated Prefill/Decode Tensor parallelism: TP=8 on Prefill and Decode KV connector: NixlConnector with HMA Prefill model runner: V1 Prefill speculative decoding: disabled Decode model runner: V2 Decode speculative decoding: DSpark, num_speculative_tokens=7 Reasoning parser: deepseek_v4 KV load failure policy: fail ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug After a failed NIXL/HMA receive, DeepSeek-V4 can return HTTP 200 with corrupted tokens in `reasoning` and an empty `content` field. Clients that read only `choices[].message.content` see an apparently empty response. Disabling thinking exposes the corrupted output in `content` instead. #### Reproduction Use disaggregated serving with DSpark disabled on Prefill and enabled on Decode. Prefill arguments: ```sh --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \ --kv-transfer-config \ '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}' ``` Decode arguments: ```sh --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config \ '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}' \ --kv-transfer-config \ '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}' ``` Send chat-completion requests with `max_tokens=128` using: 1. the default request; 2. thinking explicitly enabled; 3. thinking explicitly disabled; and 4. reasoning parsing disabled. On [`793ca6998`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/793ca6998), the asymmetric configuration fails the NIXL compatibility handshake. No KV transfer completes successfully, but the requests resume decoding. #### Expected behavior With `kv_load_failure_policy="fail"`, a failed NIXL compatibility handshake or KV receive should terminate the request with an error. The API must not return HTTP 200 or expose generated tokens in either `content` or `reasoning`. #### Actual behavior A four-mode matrix ran eight requests per mode: | Request mode | HTTP 200 with 128 tokens | `content` | `reasoning` | |---|---:|---|---| | default | 8/8 | empty | corrupted output | | thinking enabled | 8/8 | empty | corrupted output | | thinking disabled | 8/8 | corrupted output | empty | | reasoning parsing disabled | 8/8 | corrupted output | empty | All 32 requests generated 128 tokens. The apparent empty output in the first two modes is therefore response-field routing, not an absence of generation. #### Cause The failed HMA receive is reported as receive completion without a request-level failure reaching the scheduler, so Decode resumes with missing KV data and generates corrupted tokens. When thinking is enabled, the DeepSeek-V4 responses contain corrupted tokens in `reasoning` while `content` is empty. This is consistent with response parsing treating the generated text as reasoning, but the exact parser mechanism has not been isolated. The field split changes how the KV corruption is exposed; it does not show that parsing caused the KV failure. The fix proposed in [PR #52232](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52232) is model-agnostic and is expected to prevent this DeepSeek-V4/DSpark failure by terminating the request before output parsing. #### Related work - [Issue #52234](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52234) reports the underlying NIXL/HMA receive failure returning HTTP 200 with corrupted tokens. - [PR #52232](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52232) proposes model-agnostic request-level failure propagation. Although its serving regression uses Gemma, the fix is expected to cover this DeepSeek-V4/DSpark case as well. - [PR #49230](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49230) validates NIXL speculative configuration compatibility and provides the deterministic handshake-failure trigger used by this reproduction. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

``` </details> ### 🐛 Describe the bug Since the FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3 bump (#50892) wired `set_autotune_process_group` into `kernel_warmup.flashinfer_autotune` (design from #48714), **multi-node startup deadlocks deterministically during FlashInfer autotuning** on clusters whose inter-node transport is host-staged NCCL over ethernet (no GPUDirect RDMA) — here: 6× NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark class, sm_121, aarch64), 200 GbE RoCE fabric, serving `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` with TP=2 × PP=3. **Fingerprint** (identical across every reproduction): - Every rank completes the first `mxfp8_gemm` autotune round (`Tuning mxfp8_gemm: 100%|… 16/16`). - Exactly one rank of a TP pair then prints `Tuning mxfp8_gemm: 0%| | 0/16` for the next round; its TP peer never enters that round. - Both ranks of the pair sit in `futex_do_wait` (one at ~50% CPU, the peer at ~20%), GPU 0%. - All other ranks park at the barrier; EngineCore emits `shm_broadcast … No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds` once per minute forever. Startup never completes; no error, no traceback. The ranks desynchronize between tuning rounds, after which the cross-rank per-tactic timing collective blocks forever — one participant is inside the round-N profiling loop, the other never joined it. **Reproduction matrix** — the deadlock is independent of everything except the vLLM version: | vLLM | FlashInfer | NCCL | JIT caches | Result | |---|---|---|---|---| | v0.27.1 (official image) | 0.6.16.post3 | pip-bundled | warm | deadlock | | v0.27.1 (official image) | 0.6.16.post3 | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | nightly `dev18+g3d204dfda` | 0.6.16.post3 | system 2.30.7 | cold | deadlock | | nightly `dev18+g3d204dfda` | **0.6.17** (forced) | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | source build `dev54+gb96bcd0b4` | 0.6.18 | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | pre-#50892 build `0.26.1rc1.dev247` (Aug 2) | 0.6.17 | same | warm | **tunes clean** | The Aug-2 build uses the previous flow (distributed ⇒ tune on every rank, no process group, no cache broadcast) and completes the identical tuning workload on the identical hardware every time. **Workarounds validated on this cluster:** - `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS=mxfp8_gemm` — startup completes, but the un-tuned `FlashInferCutlassMxfp8LinearKernel` costs ~35% single-stream throughput (9.0 tok/s vs 14.4 tok/s tuned). - Patching `flashinfer_autotune` back to per-rank tuning (no `set_autotune_process_group`, no cache broadcast) — autotune completes on all 6 ranks and restores full performance (14.4–14.5 tok/s) on current main (`dev54+gb96bcd0b4`). Note: the synchronized flow already contains a mitigation for one hang trigger (`randomize_inputs=True` for EP ranks receiving no tokens) — this is a second, different trigger in the same design. I'll open a PR adding an opt-out env (`VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_DISTRIBUTED_SYNC=0`, default keeps current behavior) that restores the per-rank flow for affected fabrics. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

### 🐛 Describe the bug I think there is an off-by-one error in the scheduler's `self.scheduler_config.disable_chunked_mm_input` logic. `_try_schedule_encoder_inputs` in `Scheduler` guards against splitting a multimodal item across prefill chunks like this: ```python if ( self.scheduler_config.disable_chunked_mm_input and num_computed_tokens < start_pos # (A) and (num_computed_tokens + num_new_tokens) < (start_pos + num_encoder_tokens) # (B) ): num_new_tokens = max(0, start_pos - (num_computed_tokens + shift_computed_tokens)) break ``` Check (A) is causing this statement to incorrectly return False when `num_computed_tokens == start_pos`. If `num_computed_tokens == start_pos` then the tokens after `num_computed_tokens` are exactly the start of the next multi-modal item, but (A) returns False so the (B) isn't checked and the multi-modal item might get chunked. This issue is made worse by the fact if the check does fire when `num_computed_tokens < start_pos` then `num_computed_tokens` will become `start_pos`, and we will therefore hit this issue if we can't fit the multi-modal item into the token budget on the second attempt. This can silently break models with bidirectional attention, since incorrect multi-modal splitting will prevent tokens that should be able to cross-attend from cross-attending. ### Reproduction We can observe the error by testing the function directly: ```python from types import SimpleNamespace from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler START, LENGTH = 3, 766 def request(): # Fake multimodal item of length `LENGTH` offset at `START` pos = SimpleNamespace(offset=START, length=LENGTH, is_embed=None, get_num_embeds=lambda: LENGTH, get_embeds_indices_in_range=lambda a, b: (a, b)) return SimpleNamespace(has_encoder_inputs=True, request_id="r0", mm_features=[SimpleNamespace(mm_position=pos, identifier="img0", modality="image")]) def sched(): # Fake scheduler `self` with disable_chunked_mm_input=True return SimpleNamespace( scheduler_config=SimpleNamespace(disable_chunked_mm_input=True), is_encoder_decoder=False, ec_connector=None, encoder_cache_manager=SimpleNamespace( check_and_update_cache=lambda r, i: False, can_allocate=lambda r, i, b, n: True)) def ask(num_computed_tokens, num_new_tokens): # Ask how many tokens the scheduler will actually let this request run this step. # given we have done `num_computed_tokens` and can afford to do up to `num_new_tokens` more return Scheduler._try_schedule_encoder_inputs( sched(), request(), num_computed_tokens, num_new_tokens, 100_000, # stubbed encoder_compute_budget 0, # stubbed shift_computed_tokens )[1] # Works: We can don't have room for the image so it only allows 3 new tokens print(ask(0, 500)) # 3 # Breaks: the scheduler says we can go ahead and compute up to token 500, but this will # split the image since it ends on position 766 print(ask(3, 500)) # 500 ``` ### Fix As far as I can tell changing it to `num_computed_tokens <= start_pos` will fix the issue Claude thinks (A) can be deleted. I am hesitant to endorse that since I don't fully understand the logic and I am not sure why (A) was put there in the first place, but I here is its reasoning: (A) can also just be deleted, and I believe that is equivalent in normal operation. If the guard is working then the only reachable states are: | `num_computed_tokens` | meaning | (B) | |---|---|---| | `< start_pos` | before the item | decides | | `== start_pos` | at the item, nothing of it computed | decides | | `>= start_pos + length` | item already fully computed | already False, since the left side alone is >= the right | So (B) rules out the "already processed" case by itself and (A) adds nothing except excluding the boundary. The only state where the two forms differ is `start_pos < num_computed_tokens < start_pos + length`, i.e. resuming *inside* an item, which I think is only reachable with prefix caching. Deferring there seems right too for a bidirectional model -- the remainder of the item should not be split either -- but that path is reasoned about rather than tested, so `<=` is the change I would suggest. Either way it should not be possible to starve a request: `compute_mm_encoder_budget` guarantees `max_num_batched_tokens >= max_tokens_per_mm_item` whenever `disable_chunked_mm_input` is set, so a request scheduled first in a step always has room for a whole item, and a request given zero tokens hits `continue` rather than `break`, so the rest of the batch keeps moving. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [Bug]: NVFP4 MoE monolithic backend (trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe) produces semantically corrupt output for non-gated ReLU² MoE (Nemotron-3-Nano) on SM100; flashinfer_cutlass is correct on the same GPU
signals.text: ## Summary Serving `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4` (NemotronH hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE, ModelOpt NVFP4, FP8 KV cache) with default backend selection on **SM100-family GPUs (tested: B200)** produces grammatically fluent but semantically corrupted output — 100% deterministic under greedy decoding. The same checkpoint on the same vLLM version is **correct on SM120 (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell)**. An A/B/A experiment on the same B200 isolates the fault to the auto-selected **`FLASHINFER_TRTLLM` monolithic NVFP4 MoE backend**: adding `--moe-backend=flashinfer_cutlass` fully fixes the output on the same GPU with the same checkpoint; reverting to the default reproduces the broken logprobs bit-identically. ## Environment - vLLM v0.27.0 (the relevant dispatch code is byte-identical in v0.26.0; the flashinfer pin changed 0.6.14 → 0.6.16.post3 between the tags) - flashinfer-python 0.6.16.post3 (per `requirements/cuda.txt`) - Broken: B200 (compute capability 10.0). Clean: RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (12.0) - Model: `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4` — non-gated ReLU² MoE, 128 experts, top-6, sigmoid+bias grouped top-k with `n_group=1`, `hidden_size=2688`, `kv_cache_quant_algo: FP8`, `group_size: 16` - TP=1, PP=1, otherwise default flags ## Reproduction ```bash vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4 --tensor-parallel-size 1 curl -s localhost:8000/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4","prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":16,"temperature":0}' ``` Expected: `Paris…` — Actual on B200 with the default backend: `**"The Last of Us"** (2013) – a` Other 100%-deterministic failures at temperature 0: `Question: What is 2+2? Answer:` never contains `4`; the model cannot continue `1, 2, 3, 4,`. ## Evidence Top-5 logprobs for `The capital of France is` (greedy, 1 token), same B200, same checkpoint: | MoE backend | top-5 logprobs | |---|---| | default (`FLASHINFER_TRTLLM` monolithic) | `' **' -2.0724`, `'.' -2.3224`, `' ' -2.5099`, `',' -2.7599`, `'**' -2.8849` — no content token in the top-5 | | `--moe-backend=flashinfer_cutlass` | `' Paris' -0.0278` — healthy | Two forensic details: 1. **A/B/A determinism**: switching back to the default reproduces the broken logprobs **bit-identically to 10 decimal places** across restarts — this is a deterministic contract/kernel defect, not a race. 2. **The broken logits sit on a 1/16 lattice**: the gaps between the top-5 raw logits are exactly 4/16, 3/16, 4/16, 2/16. Healthy bf16 logits don't do that; it suggests the MoE contribution to the residual stream is coarsely mis-scaled/degenerate rather than "wrong but rich" — pointing at scale application rather than e.g. wrong expert selection. During the healthy `flashinfer_cutlass` run, every other SM100-default path was still active (trtllm-gen FP8-Q attention, CuTe-DSL dense NVFP4 GEMMs), so those are exonerated; the defect is fully contained in what `--moe-backend` swaps. ## Analysis (v0.27.0 tree) Selection chain: `ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE` → `select_nvfp4_moe_backend` (`vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/nvfp4.py`) tries `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM` first. `TrtLlmNvFp4ExpertsMonolithic._supports_current_device()` requires `is_device_capability_family(100)` — which is why SM120 never runs this path (matching the clean/broken hardware split) — and `_supports_no_act_and_mul()` returns True with the comment "(i.e. Nemotron-Nano)", making this model the primary user of the non-gated variant. The monolithic bundle differs from the modular `flashinfer_cutlass` path in several coupled ways; the defect must live in one of these: 1. **Hidden-size padding contract**: expert weights zero-padded 2688 → 2816 (`round_up(…, 256)`), activations padded at runtime and the output sliced back; after `nvfp4_block_scale_interleave` + epilogue tile shuffle, each row has 168 real + 8 padded scale groups. A scale offset/stride mismatch here best fits the 1/16-lattice logits. 2. **Non-gated (ReLU²) scale plumbing**: `g1_scale_c = a2_gscale.clone()`, `output1_scale_scalar = 1/a2_scale`, `output1_scale_gate_scalar = w13_scale_2 * a13_scale` — gate-slot scalars reused for a MoE that has no gate half; the contract with the flashinfer kernel is implicit. 3. **In-kernel routing**: `flashinfer.fused_moe.trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` computes DeepSeekV3-style routing internally (degenerate `n_group=1`, top-6 of 128, fp32 sigmoid+bias) vs vLLM's own `ops.grouped_topk` on the modular path. 4. **Activation scale layout**: linear (non-swizzled) — unique to this backend. 5. **`routing_replay_out` kwarg** (new call-site argument in v0.27.0) ties behavior to the installed flashinfer signature. ## Suggested immediate mitigation Until the monolithic non-gated path passes a numeric parity test, `TrtLlmNvFp4ExpertsMonolithic._supports_no_act_and_mul()` should return False so auto-selection falls back to `FLASHINFER_CUTLASS` (verified correct for this model on both SM100 and SM120). Longer-term: a CI parity test (monolithic vs modular vs QDQ emulation) on a small non-gated ReLU² MoE with hidden size **not** divisible by 256 would catch this entire defect class. User workaround until then: `--moe-backend=flashinfer_cutlass`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug **Issue**: Running DSv3 with BF16 KV throws an error during JIT due to incompatible argument types. For context, this stems from two interlinked problems: 1. Issue 1: pure causal prefills are currently always run with a **FP8** PS ASM kernel, no matter the KV dtype. 1. Fix: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48712 2. Issue 2 (this issue): BF16 causal prefills in ROCM_AITER_FA (with Opus) fails during JIT. Since issue 1 ensures that causal prefills are never routed to the BF16 Opus kernel, we don't see this issue by default. This is fixed in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48712. **This means that during causal prefills, BF16 KV is truncated to FP8 and then run through an FP8 kernel. This is not correct.** ### Profiling proof of this issue Running the default MLA backend with BF16 KV: ``` docker run --rm --name repro-mla \ --init --network host --ipc host --privileged \ --cap-add SYS_PTRACE --security-opt seccomp=unconfined \ --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 --shm-size 256G \ --group-add video --group-add render \ --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri --device /dev/infiniband \ -v /sys:/sys \ -v "/root/.cache/huggingface/:/root/.cache/huggingface" \ -e HF_HOME=/root/.cache/huggingface -e HF_TOKEN=$HF_TOKEN \ -e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 -e HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER=0 \ -e VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \ vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-ac7509e2b1db40fec2f03dde1ed4e9dfdc2338c9 \ deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3-0324 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 --max-model-len 16K ``` **Causal prefills: FP8 asm kernel is running!** This is not what we would expect with BF16 KV with parent: In contrast, chunked prefills run both the causal and non-causal part with the (correct) BF16 AITER FA impl: So pure causal prefills have their BF16 KV are truncated to FP8 and ran in lower precision! ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [Bug]: MRv2: --enable-prefix-caching (mamba_cache_mode 'all') + dspark spec decode crashes at startup — prev_last_scheduled_idx never passed by MambaHybridAttnMetadata
signals.text: ### Your current environment ```text vLLM version: v0.27.1 (release tarball, built from source; commit 6e448d0ea9) Platform: Linux aarch64 — NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121a), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.10.0a0+cu130 GPU count: 1 (TP=1) Model: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 (NemotronHForCausalLM, hybrid Mamba2 + full attention, declares SupportsMambaPrefixCaching) Draft: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark (dspark, num_speculative_tokens=4) ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug On Model Runner V2 (which `dspark` forces via `use_v2_model_runner`, `vllm/config/vllm.py:594-600`), passing `--enable-prefix-caching` without an explicit `--mamba-cache-mode` auto-selects `mamba_cache_mode='all'` for NemotronH (`vllm/model_executor/models/config.py:615-619`), and the engine then **crashes at startup during CUDA graph capture**: ```python (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] AssertionError (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 332, in _initialize_kv_caches (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] self.model_executor.compile_or_warm_up_model() (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] File ".../vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py", line 326, in capture (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] forward_fn(CUDAGraphMode.NONE) # PIECEWISE warmup, for_capture=False (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] File ".../vllm/v1/worker/gpu/attn_utils.py", line 589, in build_attn_metadata (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] metadata = attn_metadata_builder.build(...) # no prev_last_scheduled_idx (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] File ".../vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/mamba_mixer2.py", line 985, in conv_ssm_forward (EngineCore pid=217) ERROR [core.py:1349] assert block_idx_last_scheduled_token_prev_step_d is not None ``` Full reproduce command (extracted from the API server log): ```bash vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":4}' \ --mamba-backend flashinfer \ --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype float16 \ --mamba-cache-philox-rounds 5 \ --enable-mamba-cache-stochastic-rounding \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 --max-num-seqs 3 \ --async-scheduling --trust-remote-code ``` (Also crashes without the mamba-backend/stochastic-rounding extras; `mamba_cache_mode='all'` + spec decode is the trigger. Same crash with `--mamba-backend triton`.) ### Root cause In MRv2, `MambaHybridAttnMetadata.get_extra_attn_kwargs` (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py:43-56`) forwards only `num_accepted_tokens` and `num_decode_draft_tokens_cpu` to `Mamba2AttentionMetadataBuilder.build()` — it never passes `prev_last_scheduled_idx`. Consequently `_compute_common_metadata` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mamba_attn.py:504-513`) leaves `block_idx_last_scheduled_token_prev_step = None`, and the decode branch of `conv_ssm_forward` asserts when `mamba_cache_mode == "all"` and `num_spec > 0`. The legacy V1 runner handles this correctly: it allocates `self.mamba_prev_last_scheduled_idx` when `mamba_cache_mode == "all" and num_spec_tokens > 0` and passes it through (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:948-951` and `:2518-2525`). Only the MRv2 path (`model_states/mamba_hybrid.py`) is missing the wiring — consistent with MRv2 having only 'align' support wired so far (#42406). ### Expected behavior Either of: 1. MRv2 passes `prev_last_scheduled_idx` so `'all'` + spec decode works, or 2. `'all'` + spec decode is rejected/falls back to `'align'` at config validation time, instead of an assertion crash during engine init. Option 2 matches the direction from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39809 (that issue covered the V1-runner crashes on v0.19.0; this is the MRv2 equivalent on v0.27.1 — a different assert site). ### Additional context Workaround confirmed working on the same hardware/model: ```bash --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align ``` Engine starts, dspark stays active, prefix cache hits verified end-to-end (identical 37.6k-token prompt: cold prefill 5.71 s → warm 0.85 s, ~33.3k tokens served from cache, byte-identical outputs at temperature 0). FYI for hybrid users: with this model/KV config the scheduler block size is forced to 2304 tokens (mamba page size vs fp8 attention KV bytes, `vllm/platforms/interface.py:895-918`), and `use_eagle()` (true for dspark) holds back one block in `last_cache_position` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:389-394`), so prompts shorter than ~2 blocks (~4.6k tokens) never register a hit — worth documenting even once 'all' mode is fixed.

signals.title: [Bug]: Silent generation stall (Avg generation throughput drops to 0.0, no errors, /health and /v1/chat/completions still return 200) on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B / Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 / Qwen3.5-122B-A10B across v0.18.0, v0.19.0, v0.25.1
signals.text: ### Your current environment ## Environment - **vLLM versions affected:** v0.18.0, v0.19.0, v0.25.1 - **GPUs:** 8x NVIDIA H200 - **Models:** - Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (TP=8) - Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (TP=8) - Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (TP=4, 2 replicas/pods) - **Orchestration:** Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) Self-Managed 3.4.1, channel stable-3.x, deployed as KServe/InferenceService pods ## Launch parameters **Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (2 pods):** ``` --tensor-parallel-size 4 --limit-mm-per-prompt {"image":{"count":5}} --mm-encoder-tp-mode data --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 131072 --enable-chunked-prefill --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-seqs 16 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-parallel-loading-workers 16 --trust-remote-code ``` **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B / Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8:** ``` --tensor-parallel-size 8 --limit-mm-per-prompt {"image":{"count":5}} --mm-encoder-tp-mode data --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 65536 --enable-chunked-prefill --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-seqs 16 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-parallel-loading-workers 16 --trust-remote-code ``` ## Environment variables Same across all three affected versions: ``` XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp/.cache HF_HOME=/tmp/hf_home VLLM_CACHE_ROOT=/tmp/vllm FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_DIR=/tmp/flashinfer HOME=/tmp TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/.triton FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=* TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/torchinductor USER=arge LOGNAME=arge ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary We are hitting a silent hang / deadlock in vLLM's engine loop where token generation stops completely with no exception, no crash, and no log error. The engine keeps responding to `/metrics` and `/health` with 200 OK, so the pod is never restarted by the orchestrator's liveness probe, but no request is ever completed after the stall begins — requests simply queue up forever (`Waiting` count grows, `Running` count does not drain). This has been observed across **three different vLLM versions** (v0.18.0, v0.19.0, v0.25.1) and **three different models** (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), all served on 8x H200 GPUs via Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI 3.4.1, channel stable-3.x). ## Environment - **vLLM versions affected:** v0.18.0, v0.19.0, v0.25.1 - **GPUs:** 8x NVIDIA H200 - **Models:** - Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (TP=8) - Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (TP=8) - Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (TP=4, 2 replicas/pods) - **Orchestration:** Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) Self-Managed 3.4.1, channel stable-3.x, deployed as KServe/InferenceService pods ## Launch parameters **Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (2 pods):** ``` --tensor-parallel-size 4 --limit-mm-per-prompt {"image":{"count":5}} --mm-encoder-tp-mode data --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 131072 --enable-chunked-prefill --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-seqs 16 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-parallel-loading-workers 16 --trust-remote-code ``` **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B / Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8:** ``` --tensor-parallel-size 8 --limit-mm-per-prompt {"image":{"count":5}} --mm-encoder-tp-mode data --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 65536 --enable-chunked-prefill --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-seqs 16 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-parallel-loading-workers 16 --trust-remote-code ``` ## Environment variables Same across all three affected versions: ``` XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp/.cache HF_HOME=/tmp/hf_home VLLM_CACHE_ROOT=/tmp/vllm FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_DIR=/tmp/flashinfer HOME=/tmp TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/.triton FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=* TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/torchinductor USER=arge LOGNAME=arge ``` ## Observed behavior From `loggers.py:273` periodic stats immediately before and after the stall (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, 2-pod deployment): ``` FO 08-13 10:48:06 [loggers.py:273] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 2351.3 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 353.0 tokens/s, Running: 4 reqs, Waiting: 1 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.7%, Prefix cache hit rate: 46.1%, MM cache hit rate: 47.6% ... FO 08-13 10:48:16 [loggers.py:273] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 230.6 tokens/s, Running: 1 reqs, Waiting: 3 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 93.3%, MM cache hit rate: 47.6% ... FO 08-13 10:48:26 [loggers.py:273] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Running: 1 reqs, Waiting: 4 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 93.3%, MM cache hit rate: 47.6% ``` Key points: - No exception, traceback, or CUDA error is ever printed. - `GET /metrics` and presumably `/health` keep returning `200 OK` throughout the stall — **this is what prevents Kubernetes/OpenShift liveness probes from restarting the pod**, so the deployment silently serves zero traffic until manually restarted. - `GPU KV cache usage` and `Prefix cache hit rate` remain static/frozen after the stall begins, consistent with the scheduler loop being alive (still logging stats) but the underlying step/generation not completing. ## Reproduction rate / conditions - Happens under production-shaped concurrent traffic (multiple concurrent chat completion requests, tool-calling + multimodal image inputs in the mix). - Occurs across TP=4 and TP=8 configurations, across dense-ish (122B-A10B, 397B-A17B) and FP8-quantized variants, so does not appear tied to a specific quantization path or TP size. ## Impact Because `/health` stays healthy, this causes **silent full-service outage** — no automated recovery, only caught by external monitoring/alerting on generation throughput or by manual pod restarts. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [Bug]: Data-parallel startup ignores DP in startup_omp_num_threads, causing CPU thread oversubscription and 15x slower weight loading (engine-ready timeout)
signals.text:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text collect_env.py could not be run interactively in the environment where this failure was captured (a batch scheduler job whose container is torn down at exit). The following is the environment as recorded from the job's own package manifest and device inventory: vLLM version : 0.26.1rc1.dev602+g65b7662d3 PyTorch : 2.13.0+cu130 CUDA runtime : 13.0.2 Python : 3.12.3 OS : Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64) GPU driver : 580.167.08 GPUs : 8x NVIDIA B200 (183359 MiB each, compute capability 10.0, 148 SMs); 4 GPUs used by this run CPU : Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8570, 224 logical CPUs (nproc inside the container reports 224) System memory : ~2.0 TiB Relevant packages: transformers 5.15.0 triton 3.7.1 nvidia-nccl-cu13 2.30.7 flashinfer-python 0.6.16.post3 flashinfer-cubin 0.6.16.post3 flashinfer-jit-cache 0.6.16.post3+cu130 compressed-tensors 0.17.0 runai-model-streamer 0.16.1 nvidia-nvshmem-cu13 3.4.5 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary `startup_omp_num_threads()` divides the machine's CPU count by the number of *local worker processes within one engine*, with no term for data parallelism. With `--data-parallel-size N` on a single node, N engine cores each independently claim the entire CPU count for their torch thread pool. On a 224-CPU node at DP=4 that is 4 x 224 = 896 torch threads competing for 224 CPUs. The visible consequence is a ~15x slowdown in model weight loading, which in turn blows the engine-ready deadline and crashes startup: ``` (ApiServer_0 pid=3383311) TimeoutError: Timed out waiting for engine core processes to start. This is often caused by slow weight loading for large models. Waited 600s (configured by VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S). To increase the timeout, set the environment variable: VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S= ``` All `api_server_count` frontends raise it, followed by: ``` RuntimeError: Frontend process failed during engine core initialization. See root cause above. Failed frontend proc(s): {'ApiServer_0': None} ``` and `BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe` from each `Worker_DP{0..3}_EP{0..3}` as the executor is torn down mid-load. Note the 600s figure is vLLM's own default (`envs.py`: `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S: int = 600`). No timeout override was set for this run. ## Mechanism `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py`: ```python def startup_omp_num_threads(num_local_procs: int) -> int: return max(1, available_cpu_count() // max(1, num_local_procs)) ``` `vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py` passes `self.local_world_size`: ```python set_multiprocessing_worker_envs(self.local_world_size) ``` and `local_world_size` is derived only from tensor, pipeline, and prefill-context parallelism — the assertion just above it reads `world_size == tensor_parallel_size * pipeline_parallel_size * prefill_context_parallel_size`, with no data-parallel factor. So each engine core computes its divisor as if it were the only process on the node. This is directly observable in the failing run's log: with `--tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 4`, all four engine cores report ``` [multiproc_executor.py:149] DP group leader: node_rank=0, node_rank_within_dp=0, ... world_size=1, local_world_size=1 ``` `local_world_size=1` on a 224-CPU node yields `224 // 1 = 224` threads per engine, 896 node-wide. The function correctly early-returns when the user has already set `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, so the bug only bites the default path. ## Reproduction ```bash # upstream nightly image docker run --gpus all --ipc=host --shm-size=32g \ -v /path/to/models:/models \ vllm/vllm-openai:nightly \ vllm serve /models/Kimi-K2-Thinking-NVFP4 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --trust-remote-code \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --served-model-name kimi-k2-thinking \ --load-format runai_streamer \ --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --pipeline-parallel-size 1 \ --data-parallel-size 4 \ --max-model-len 10240 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --async-scheduling \ --compilation_config.cudagraph_mode FULL_DECODE_ONLY \ --compilation_config.max_cudagraph_capture_size 2048 \ --moe-backend flashinfer_trtllm ``` Checkpoint: `nvidia/Kimi-K2-Thinking-NVFP4` (public on Hugging Face). Hardware: single node, 4x B200, 224 logical CPUs. No `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and no `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` set. The reproducer needs a high core count and a checkpoint made of many small tensors; see "Why block-quantized checkpoints amplify this" below. ### Expected behavior Startup completes. Each engine's torch thread pool is sized so that the aggregate across all local engines does not exceed the machine's CPU count. ### Actual behavior Weight loading takes 1822s and startup fails at the 600s engine-ready deadline. From the failing run: ``` [serve.py:123] Defaulting api_server_count to data_parallel_size (4). ... (Worker_DP0_EP0) [gpu_model_runner.py:5483] Model loading took 154.87 GiB memory and 1822.406850 seconds ``` The frontends abandon startup at 600s while the workers are still loading; the load would have needed 1822s, i.e. ~1222s past the deadline it had to meet. ## Single-variable A/B isolating the thread count Two runs, identical image, identical checkpoint, identical flags, same DP=4 topology, same 224-CPU node class. The only difference is whether `OMP_NUM_THREADS` is set, which is exactly the variable the early-return in `set_multiprocessing_worker_envs` controls: | `OMP_NUM_THREADS` | threads/engine | node-wide | weight load | server startup | outcome | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | unset (default) | 224 | 896 | **1822.4 s** | never completes | `TimeoutError` at 600 s | | `56` (= 224/4) | 56 | 224 | **118.3 s** | 360 s | serves normally, 1921 tok/s | **15.4x on weight loading from thread count alone.** The load time is highly reproducible: three independent runs on the default path measured 1822.4s, 1816.7s, and 1815.5s (0.38% spread). A dose-response across topologies on the same 224-CPU node class, all block-quantized checkpoints: | topology | threads/worker | node-wide threads | weight load | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DP=1 | 56 | 224 | 56 s | | DP=4, `OMP_NUM_THREADS=56` | 56 | 224 | 118 s | | DP=8, `OMP_NUM_THREADS=56` | 56 | 448 | 671 s | | DP=4, default | 224 | 896 | 1822 s | | DP=8, default | 224 | 1792 | 2059 s | On a 144-CPU node the same DP=4 configuration loads in 230s — fewer cores means a smaller divisor numerator, so less oversubscription. Higher core count makes this *worse*, which is the signature of the divisor being wrong rather than of a resource shortage. ## Why block-quantized checkpoints amplify this The slowdown scales with tensor *count*, not bytes. The NVFP4 checkpoint above deserializes into ~277k small tensors, most just above torch's internal `GRAIN_SIZE` threshold for parallelizing an elementwise op — so nearly every tensor pays full thread-pool dispatch overhead against an oversubscribed pool. Equivalent bf16 checkpoints load as ~51 large tensors and are essentially unaffected; FP8 variants of the same models also pass. So this reproduces most sharply on NVFP4/MXFP4/block-quantized weights. ## Why this surfaces as a crash only with `vllm serve` Worth noting for anyone trying to reproduce via the module entrypoint: the slowdown occurs either way, but only `vllm serve` turns it into a hard failure. `vllm serve` defaults `api_server_count` to `data_parallel_size` (in `vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py`), which routes through `run_multi_api_server` and the externally-managed client path, where `MPClient` polls with a `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` budget. `python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server` never references `api_server_count` — its `__main__` calls `uvloop.run(run_server(args))` unconditionally — and takes the self-managed path, where `wait_for_engine_startup` polls at `STARTUP_POLL_PERIOD_MS` and `continue`s indefinitely with only `logger.debug` output. On that path the same configuration silently absorbed a 2010s startup with no error at all. A related detail on the deadline itself: the poll sits *inside* `while identities:`, so each received ready-message restarts the budget. It is a per-message idle timeout rather than a cumulative startup deadline. Because this load emits no intermediate ready messages, the very first poll exceeds 600s anyway. ## Regression range Bisected with per-commit wheels from `https://wheels.vllm.ai/`, holding the base image, checkpoint, flags, and all other dependency versions fixed: - last known good: `52c0e3cb08b8178829e1f2db4ac90e9bb98c8a5f` (`0.26.1rc1.dev327+g52c0e3cb0`) — weight load 114.8 s, serves normally - first bad: `7635a9002baecca64909dbcf8b1d461d26fb879d` (`0.26.1rc1.dev328+g7635a9002`) — weight load 1961.7 s That boundary is PR #49919 ("[Core] Explicitly manage torch CPU threads in workers"), which introduced `startup_omp_num_threads`. **Caveat, stated explicitly:** this bisect pair was measured at `--tensor-parallel-size 4` with no data parallelism. It brackets the introduction of the explicit thread-management code, and shows that code made this configuration much slower; it does not by itself isolate the missing DP term. The DP-specific evidence is the A/B and dose-response tables above. ## Suggested fix Include the local data-parallel replica count in the divisor, so the aggregate thread count across co-located engines respects the CPU budget. Both fields are already available on `ParallelConfig` (`data_parallel_size_local` and `local_world_size`), so the executor can pass `local_world_size * max(1, data_parallel_size_local)` instead of `local_world_size` alone. A node-wide accounting would be more robust still, since headless/multi-node layouts can place a differing number of engines per node. ## Prior art on this knob - PR #6109 (merged 2024) originally set a blanket `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` for the multiprocessing GPU executor; PR #49919 superseded that with explicit per-worker thread management. - PR #22773 (closed, not merged) addressed OMP thread selection for the CPU backend's `VLLM_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND` path — a different executor, but the same class of problem. ## Workaround for users hitting this Set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` explicitly to `available_cpus / (local engines x workers per engine)` before launching. The early-return in `set_multiprocessing_worker_envs` then leaves it alone. Raising `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` is *not* a good workaround — it converts the crash into a silent multi-fold startup regression. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the documentation and FAQ for help before opening a new issue. --- _This issue was drafted with assistance from the `opus` AI model._

signals.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4 FlashMLA sparse prefill phase1.cuh:614 on H20-3e TP8 at ~161K context
signals.text: ### Your current environment - **GPU**: 8× NVIDIA H20-3e - **vLLM**: 0.26.0 - **Image**: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.26.0-w4a16-patched2` - **Model**: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-w4a16` - **Parallelism**: TP=8, expert parallel enabled - **KV cache dtype**: FP8 - **Block size**: 256 - **Max model length**: 614400 - **Chunked prefill**: enabled (`max_num_batched_tokens=8192` from startup log) - **Max num seqs**: 32 - **Speculative decoding**: ```json { "method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 7, "draft_sample_method": "greedy" } ``` Relevant launch arguments: ```bash vllm serve /data/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-w4a16 \ --tensor-parallel-size=8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --max-model-len=614400 \ --gpu-memory-utilization=0.85 \ --kv-cache-dtype=fp8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-num-seqs=32 \ --block-size=256 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser=deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config='{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}' ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` crashes during the FlashMLA **SM90 sparse prefill** path with a TMA descriptor initialization failure. All 8 TP workers report the same assertion and the EngineCore exits. This looks related to #49922 / #50660 / #49883, but I am filing separately because this reproduction is on **H20-3e, TP=8** and occurs at only about **161K context**, rather than only at very large (>600K) prefills. Immediately before the crash, FlashMLA prints: ```text TMA Desc Addr: 0x7ffcc4269000 format 9 dim 3 gmem_address 0 globalDim (512,64,0,1,1) ... Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor Assertion `res == CUresult::CUDA_SUCCESS` failed (/workspace/.deps/flashmla-src/csrc/sm90/prefill/sparse/instantiations/../phase1.cuh:614) ``` The worker traceback reaches: ```text vllm/models/deepseek_v4/attention.py -> forward_mqa vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/flashmla.py -> _forward_prefill vllm/third_party/flashmla/flash_mla_interface.py -> flash_mla_sparse_fwd flash_mla_cuda.sparse_prefill_fwd -> sm90/prefill/sparse/phase1.cuh:614 ``` All TP workers then fail with: ```text RuntimeError: Assertion error (/workspace/.deps/flashmla-src/csrc/sm90/prefill/sparse/instantiations/../phase1.cuh:614): Assertion `res == CUresult::CUDA_SUCCESS` failed. ``` ### Scheduler state at the failing step The V1 engine dump at the crash shows two cached/running requests: ```text num_computed_tokens=[27019, 161008] num_scheduled_tokens: request A: 8 request B: 312 total_num_scheduled_tokens=320 ``` So one request had already computed about **27K** tokens, while the second had computed about **161K** tokens and was scheduled for another **312** tokens in that step. This appears to be a **mixed decode + chunked-prefill** iteration, which may be a useful trigger condition to investigate. I am not claiming that mixed batching is the root cause; this is only the scheduler state captured at the failing iteration. ### Memory does not look exhausted Startup reported: ```text Available KV cache memory: 92.93 GiB GPU KV cache size: 6,819,501 tokens Maximum concurrency for 614,400 tokens per request: 11.10x ``` The scheduler dump at the failing iteration reported: ```text kv_cache_usage=0.0100178 ``` So this does not look like a KV-cache OOM condition. ### Reproducibility I have observed the same `phase1.cuh:614` / `Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor` crash more than once on this deployment. The service starts normally and can serve requests before the crash occurs. ### Related issues / possible fix This looks very close to #49922 and #50660. In #49922, `de6ec294ef07` / #49302 is discussed and reported to fix the zero-query / phantom-request condition on other hardware. I have **not yet verified** whether `v0.26.0-w4a16-patched2` contains that change, nor whether cherry-picking it fixes this H20-3e reproduction. If maintainers believe this is the same root cause, I am happy for this issue to be marked duplicate. The main additional data point here is that the same TMA descriptor shape (`gmem_address=0`, zero extent) is reproducible on **H20-3e TP8 around 161K context** during a mixed decode/chunked-prefill step. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] I searched existing issues and found #49922, #50660 and #49883. I am filing this separately because of the different hardware and significantly lower context length / scheduler state at failure.

signals.title: [Feature]: Native OCP MXFP6 execution on NVIDIA SM120
signals.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch vLLM can load OCP MXFP6 checkpoints through Quark, but CUDA execution currently uses software emulation. PR [#21166](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/21166) added the format and emulation support and left native OCP MX kernels as follow-up work. We built [mxfp6-sm120](https://github.com/Nekofish-L/mxfp6_sm120), a BSD-licensed PyTorch CUDA extension for native OCP W6A8 execution on NVIDIA SM120. It keeps weights in packed MXFP6 E3M2 with UE8M0 scales, quantizes FP16/BF16 activations to MXFP8 E4M3 at runtime, and accumulates in FP32. The current implementation includes: - a general Dense GEMM operator; - a Qwen3.5 routed-MoE path covering routing, W1, activation processing, W2, shared-expert combine, and final reduction; - persistent workspaces and CUDA Graph replay for the tested execution paths. A public vLLM v0.25.1 reproducer loads and serves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on two RTX 5090 GPUs with tensor parallel size 2. Compared with the corresponding official FP8 checkpoints, MXFP6 improved output throughput by 9.11% for Qwen3.5-27B and 16.95% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. This issue documents the working implementation and measured scope. If this evidence is not yet sufficient to evaluate an upstream contribution, we can add targeted correctness coverage, workloads, hardware configurations, or fallback tests. ### Alternatives The existing Quark software-emulation path remains a functional fallback, but it does not execute the packed weights with native SM120 MX instructions. The repository also contains a narrowly versioned vLLM compatibility patch. That patch demonstrates end-to-end integration for the two tested models; it is not proposed as an upstream patch. ### Additional context #### Public end-to-end results The public reproduction uses vLLM v0.25.1, two PIX-connected RTX 5090 GPUs, tensor parallel size 2, and four fresh service lifecycles in FP8/MXFP6/MXFP6/FP8 order. | Model and workload | FP8 output tok/s | MXFP6 output tok/s | Gain | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Qwen3.5-27B, 3000 input / 1000 output, c32 | 1229.90 | 1341.97 | **+9.11%** | | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, public `random-mm`, c4 | 678.37 | 793.33 | **+16.95%** | Standalone measurements report a 1.633x geometric-mean speedup over vLLM block-FP8 for the five measured Qwen3.5-27B Dense shapes, and 1.278x over the vLLM FP8 MoE path for the complete Qwen3.5-35B-A3B TP2 MoE layer at B16-B96. Operator, layer, and service results have different measurement boundaries and are not additive. #### Internal runtime reference We also measured the package with an internally optimized vLLM 0.25.1 stack: 22.44% higher output throughput for Qwen3.5-27B and 13.58% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On the 35B-A3B workload, 742 greedy reference cases changed full-character similarity by -0.57 percentage points and answer-section similarity by -0.32 points relative to FP8. Neither paired 95% interval detected a significant loss. This is reference-output fidelity, not task accuracy, and the internal serving results are not claims about the public reproducer. #### Reproduction and evidence - Project: https://github.com/Nekofish-L/mxfp6_sm120 - Public vLLM reproduction: https://github.com/Nekofish-L/mxfp6_sm120/tree/main/examples/vllm - Public serving result: https://github.com/Nekofish-L/mxfp6_sm120/blob/main/benchmarks/results/qwen35_public_vllm_tp2.json - Benchmark methodology: https://github.com/Nekofish-L/mxfp6_sm120/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md - Original MXFP6 format request: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/17837 - Existing format and emulation support: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/21166

signals.title: [Refactor] Refactor EPD
signals.text: ## Summary vLLM has the EPD scaffolding (`vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/`, `ECConnectorBase` with scheduler + worker roles, `ECConnectorFactory`, `ec_transfer_params` in the OpenAI layer, E→PD / E→P→D examples). But **every existing EC connector transfers synchronously and locally**, and the encode → stage → send → release flow is hard-wired to that assumption: - `ECExampleConnector` — `save_caches()` writes a safetensors file to shared disk; the consumer `start_load_caches()` reads it back. Blocking, filesystem-bound. - `ECCPUConnector` — offloads the encoder cache into a CPU mmap region on the same host. Blocking, single-host only. There is **no over-the-wire backend**: the encoder and PD instances must share a filesystem or a host. By contrast the KV path already ships pluggable network transports (`NixlConnector`, `MooncakeConnector`, … in `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/factory.py`). The EC path needs the same: a refactor that turns the single hard-coded transfer path into a **backend-agnostic pipeline** where new transports plug in cleanly. ## Goal: refactor EPD around a pluggable, async-safe transfer layer The core goal is the **refactor** — make the encoder-instance flow backend-agnostic so that supporting many transfer backends is a matter of implementing a delivery interface, not rewriting the pipeline. The first two backends to land on top of it: 1. **`ECZmqConnector`** — producer pushes the embedding over a ZMQ socket to the consumer (PD scheduler). Simple, dependency-light, works across nodes. 2. **`ECMooncakeConnector`** — RDMA transfer: the consumer registers a landing buffer and reads the embedding out of the producer's GPU buffer. High throughput for large embeddings. These backends are **asynchronous** and **cross-process**, which the current blocking `save_caches` / `start_load_caches` contract cannot express safely. The refactor exists precisely to make async, over-the-wire transfer correct — and to make the *next* backend after these two trivial to add. ## The unified post-`receive` pipeline Everything after `receive` should follow a single chain, so every backend shares one safe ordering instead of each transport re-implementing send/release: ``` receive (protocol-specific entry point) → execute_encode_pipeline → MMEncoder.encode / batch_encode → acquire encode ref → preprocess → publish metadata # shape/dtype/size, BEFORE the forward → model forward → stage embedding # sets embedding_ready after CUDA sync → release encode ref → delivery.send # ZMQ push OR Mooncake RDMA notify → release_request # only after all sends complete ``` ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

## 🐛 Describe the bug ### What happens On a preempted request, `MooncakeStoreConnector` stores **KV that does not belong to the key**. Those bytes are later read back by another request as a prefix-cache hit, loaded into the KV cache and attended over, which silently corrupts that request's output. ### Why The store is asynchronous. During a step the worker only pushes the store request onto `KVCacheStoreSendingThread`'s queue and returns; reading the blocks off the GPU and issuing the PUT happens later, on the background thread. Freeing the blocks takes an entirely separate path: in a following step the scheduler preempts the request, and core returns its blocks to the free pool within that same step, after which another request overwrites them. There is no synchronization between the two — nothing constrains when a queued job reads device memory relative to when its blocks are handed to someone else. The preemption notice does not help either. The earliest it can reach the worker is on the next step's connector metadata (`MooncakeStoreConnectorMetadata.preempted_req_ids`), and core has already freed the blocks in the very step that builds that metadata. In other words the blocks can be fully overwritten before the notice arrives, and with async scheduling the scheduler runs further ahead still. The only protection today is `request_finished()` returning `delay_free_blocks=True`, which covers the **normal completion** path only. Preemption goes the other way: `build_connector_meta()` calls `reset()` on the tracker, the blocks are freed immediately, and nothing knows that queued jobs still have to read them. ### Consequences 1. **Silent wrong results.** The poisoned key holds another request's KV, so a request that hits it attends over KV that is not its own and its output drifts unpredictably, with no error anywhere. 2. **It does not heal.** A key names a fixed token range, so once wrong bytes land under a key, every later request that hits the same prefix keeps being fed them. Contamination grows with uptime rather than decaying. 3. The more memory-constrained the deployment and the more it preempts, the more often this fires — which is exactly the deployment that wants an external KV store. ### How to reproduce Preemption has to actually happen. Configuration: - 2x H20, TP2, Qwen3-32B-FP8 - `--num-gpu-blocks-override 1024` (shrink the GPU cache to force preemption) - mooncake store backend, started cold - load: 96 requests / 48 concurrent / ~400-word prompts / `max_tokens=192` This configuration produces 162 preemptions in a single run. Nothing is visible from the outputs alone (wrong KV makes the text drift, it does not raise), so the determination is made by instrumentation. Two independent signals: **(1) Content fingerprints.** A store key names a fixed token range, so the KV under it is uniquely determined. The patch takes an 8-byte `D_pre` on the GPU **before** `batch_put` (the blocks still hold that key's own KV at that moment) and `D_post` on the destination blocks **after** `batch_get`. A disagreement means the bytes in the store are not the KV that key names, and they are already in a real request's KV blocks, about to be attended over. **(2) A scheduler-side block reallocation detector.** Recorded independently on the scheduler side: whether the blocks a store job references were reallocated to another request while that job was reading them. This signal never looks at the store's contents. The instrumentation, the load and the analysis scripts are at (instrumentation only, no behaviour changes): the fingerprint patch (`probes/fingerprint_on_main.patch`, applies on `643c125fa`), the preemption-forcing server config (`load/ab_serve.sh`), the synthetic load (`load/synth_load.py`, random-gibberish prompts so nothing dedups in the store and every save is a real `batch_put`), the orchestration for one run (`load/ab_run.sh`: cold master, server, poll `/health`, send the load) and the two analysers (`analysis/analyze_evi.py` for totals, `analysis/bad_dist.py` to split poisoned keys by `save_seq`). ### Measured `643c125fa` plus the instrumentation above, one run against a cold store, all 96 requests returned, 162 preemptions: | | | |---|---| | keys written with a fingerprint | 16,770 | | of those, written twice with differing content (excluded as ambiguous) | 0 | | read-backs checked | 16,788 | | **fingerprint mismatches** | **155** | | poisoned keys | 155 | | **requests that read wrong KV** | **1 / 96** | | jobs the scheduler-side detector flagged as "blocks reallocated while being read" | 25 | | preemptions | 162 | All 155 poisoned keys come from a single store job (`save_seq=125`), and that job is one of the 25 the scheduler-side detector flagged independently — two unrelated signals point at the same job. ### Relation to #51637 / #51662 #51637 describes a **secondary** problem derived from the same preemption scenario: a request that is rescheduled after preemption keeps its original req_id, and the store thread's bookkeeping only checks whether the req_id matches, so a leftover job from the retired generation spends the new generation's credit. The live save is silently dropped, the counter goes negative, the entry can never retire, `finished_sending` is never emitted and the blocks are held until KV starvation. #51662 fixes that. This issue is about the block lifetime itself: it never covered the preemption path to begin with. ## Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [Spec Decode][CUDA Graphs] Enables Eagle drafter support for FULL CUDA Graph mode
signals.text: ## Purpose As mentioned in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/issues/5459 and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/33341 , this PR enables **Full CUDA Graph** mode for the Eagle drafter model to improve performance. The main changes include: 1. **CUDA Graph Integration:** Wraps the drafter model with `CUDAGraphWrapper` during `load_model` and initializes the necessary keys for the dispatcher to manage graph-based execution. 2. **Graph Capture Support:** Builds dummy attention metadata during the `dummy_run` phase, which is required for successful graph capture. 3. **Dispatch:** For the first step, the draft model shares the same `uniform_decode` with target model and basically has the same `batch_desc` and `cudagraph_mode`, while for the following steps, the `uniform_decode_query_len` will be set to 1 and `uniform_decode` to `True`, making it possible to have separate `cudagraph_keys`. 4. **Metadata Correction:** Corrects the memory address handling for `query_start_loc` and `slot_mapping` within the attention metadata. 5. **Bug Fix:** Adjusts CUDA graph capture sizes to resolve a runtime error that occurred when `num_speculative_tokens` was set to 2. Also fix `prepare_inputs_padded` and `prepare_next_token_ids_padded` for padding issues. Collectively, these changes allow the Eagle drafter to leverage the performance benefits of Full CUDA Graph mode, enhancing throughput for speculative decoding. ## Test Plan The feature was tested by running the model with the following configuration: - `num_speculative_tokens=2` (and also validated with `3/4/5`) - `cudagraph_mode="FULL"` (and also validated with `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` and `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`) ## Test Result The model's acceptance rate in Full CUDA Graph mode is consistent with the results from eager mode. For `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`: ``` ... signals.title: Fused BMM+FP8 quant Triton kernel for MLA _v_up_proj (forward_mqa path)
signals.text: ## Purpose Adds a Triton kernel that fuses the batched matrix multiply in `_v_up_proj` with FP8 static quantization on the MLA decode path (`forward_mqa`), eliminating a bf16 memory round-trip. **Depends on #36205** — will rebase onto main once that merges. ## Problem After #36205, MLA decode quantization is two-step: 1. `_v_up_proj` does `torch.bmm` → writes bf16 to memory 2. Separate `static_scaled_fp8_quant` kernel → reads bf16, writes fp8 This is 3 memory ops (write bf16 + read bf16 + write fp8). ## Solution A single Triton kernel (`bmm_fp8_quant`) that does the BMM and quantizes to FP8 in one pass — the bf16 intermediate never leaves GPU registers. This reduces it to 1 memory write (fp8). ### Changes - **`vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_bmm_fp8.py`** (new): Triton fused BMM+FP8 kernel - **`vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py`**: Modified `_v_up_proj` to accept `output_scale`/`quant_output` and call fused kernel; updated `forward_impl` to use fused path for FP8 static quant decode - **`tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py`** (new): Unit tests ### Scope - FP8 static per-tensor quant on the standard (non-AIter) BMM path - NVFP4 fusion for `_v_up_proj` is a follow-up (requires block-wise scales, different kernel structure) - Prefill path (`forward_mha`) unchanged ## Test Results (H100, sm90) ``` tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py::test_bmm_fp8_quant_correctness[dtype0-128-512-1-16] PASSED tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py::test_bmm_fp8_quant_correctness[dtype0-128-512-7-16] PASSED tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py::test_bmm_fp8_quant_correctness[dtype0-128-512-32-16] PASSED tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py::test_bmm_fp8_quant_correctness[dtype0-128-512-256-16] PASSED tests/v1/attention/ops/test_triton_bmm_fp8.py::test_bmm_fp8_quant_shapes PASSED ======================== 5 passed in 2.27s ========================= ``` Related: #35792

signals.title: feat(dcp, flashinfer): support FULL_DECODE_ONLY for flashinfer with DCP>1
signals.text: ## Purpose Allocate persistent buffers for DCP-related variables to enable FULL_DECODE_ONLY support. ## Test Plan ``` bash .buildkite/lm-eval-harness/run-lm-eval-gsm-vllm-baseline.sh -m Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/ -b "auto" -l 1000 -f 5 -t 4 ``` ## Test Result <!-- codex-accuracy-validation-start --> ### Full GSM8K accuracy validation (requires #48003) > [!IMPORTANT] > **PR #48003 is required for accuracy correctness.** PR #36503 alone still uses global sequence lengths for FlashInfer DCP paged-KV metadata and produces corrupted DCP output. Apply #48003 together with this PR before using FlashInfer with `decode_context_parallel_size > 1`, including `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` graph mode. Accuracy was validated with #48003 temporarily stacked on top of this PR. The run used 4x NVIDIA H20 with `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`, FlashInfer, all 1,319 GSM8K samples, 5-shot prompting, greedy decoding (`temperature=0`), `max_tokens=256`, `max_model_len=4096`, and seed 42. The local weight directory did not contain tokenizer assets, so the matching official `Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` tokenizer/config files were overlaid for evaluation. | Configuration | Correct | Accuracy | Invalid | |---|---:|---:|---:| | TP=4, DCP=1, eager | 730 / 1,319 | 55.345% | 0.227% | | TP=4, DCP=2, eager | 738 / 1,319 | 55.951% | 0.152% | | TP=4, DCP=2, `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` graph | 718 / 1,319 | 54.435% | 0.000% | Without #48003, the same DCP cases produced only 9/1,319 (0.682%) correct in eager mode and 8/1,319 (0.607%) correct in graph mode. With #48003 applied, DCP eager is +0.607 percentage points versus the TP baseline and DCP graph is -0.910 percentage points versus the TP baseline, removing the catastrophic FlashInfer DCP corruption. Graph mode also captured all 51 `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` CUDA graphs successfully. <!-- codex-accuracy-validation-end --> --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. - [ ] (Optional) Release notes update.
